evidence.title: ChatGPT-4o as a decision-support tool in a urological tumour board: a prospective evaluation
evidence.venue: Clinical & translational oncology : official publication of the Federation of Spanish Oncology Societies and of the National Cancer Institute of Mexico
evidence.outcome: Concordance of ChatGPT-4o recommendation with final MTB decision versus protocol benchmark
evidence.effect: High concordance for recommendation 79.2% (95% CI, 70.6-85.9), below the ≥80% benchmark; no attitude change (0/106); added value 13.2%
evidence.quote: High concordance was 91.5% (summarisation), 84.0% (reasoning) and 79.2% (recommendation; 95% CI, 70.6-85.9), below benchmark (Friedman χ2 = 34.756; p < 0.001; κ = 0.618).

evidence.title: Clinical Evidence and FDA Recalls of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices
evidence.outcome: Hazard of FDA recall by availability of published clinical studies at authorization
evidence.effect: Devices with missing clinical study information had higher recall hazard than devices with published clinical studies (HR, 1.39; 95% CrI, 0.84-3.52); the credible interval includes 1.
evidence.quote: Devices with missing information regarding clinical studies had a higher hazard of recall than devices with published clinical studies (HR, 1.39; 95% CrI, 0.84-3.52).

evidence.title: An Investigation of Lesion Detection Accuracy for Artificial Intelligence-Based Denoising of Low-Dose 64Cu-DOTATATE PET Imaging in Patients with Neuroendocrine Neoplasms
evidence.venue: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
evidence.outcome: Lesion detection by physician readers on AI-denoised low-dose PET versus full-dose reference, despite good image-quality metrics
evidence.effect: Image quality rated good/excellent in 32/33 PET_AI; but sensitivity 66% (78/118), false discovery rate 32% (37/115); 62% (23/37) of FPs scored as definite lesions.
evidence.quote: However, lesion detection analysis performed by physicians showed high proportions of FP and FN lesions on PET<sub>AI</sub>, highlighting the need for clinical validation of AI algorithms.

evidence.title: Empirically derived evaluation requirements for responsible deployments of AI in safety-critical settings

evidence.effect: Simulated evaluation with nurses revealed severe potential risks (degradation from misleading AI) prior to deployment despite favorable benchmark performance.
evidence.quote: The study we conducted is an example of one such evaluation which was able to empirically reveal severe potential risks prior to deployment.
evidence.sample_unit: participants (450 nursing students and 12 licensed nurses; 4125 case records analyzed)

evidence.title: Validation of an AI-based automated Knee Inflammation MRI Scoring System for assessing bone marrow lesions
evidence.effect: Baseline ICCs 0.75 and 0.85 vs two manual experts; 0.31-0.84 vs 11 readers using automated grid placement.

evidence.title: Evaluating chain-of-thought prompting in a GPT chatbot for BCID2 interpretation and stewardship: how does AI compare to human experts?
evidence.outcome: Clinical safety and adequacy of chatbot recommendations in real-world cases, rated by ID physicians

evidence.quote: The chatbot performed well in BCID2 interpretation (100% accuracy) but provided more inadequate responses in source control consideration (10% vs. 2% for ASP, p = 0.022).

evidence.title: Secure On-Premise Deployment of Open-Weights Large Language Models in Radiology: An Isolation-First Architecture with Prospective Pilot Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Frequency of critical errors (hallucinations, omissions) in LLM output by prompt task type
evidence.effect: Open-ended conclusion generation from findings produced the highest frequency of critical errors, such as clinically relevant hallucinations or omissions; source text-anchored tasks received the highest utility ratings.
evidence.quote: Source text-anchored tasks, such as report corrections or simplifications, and radiology guideline recommendations received the highest utility ratings, whereas open-ended conclusion generation based on findings resulted in the highest frequency of critical errors, such as clinically relevant hallucinations or omissions.

evidence.outcome: Share of public summaries stating clinical data supporting device performance
evidence.effect: Clinical data stated for 70.6% of 1,491 analyzed decisions; a canonical performance metric for 52.3%.
evidence.quote: Clinical data were stated for 70.6%, a canonical performance metric for 52.3%, multisite evaluation for 42.7%, and prospective or reader studies for 16.8%.
evidence.sample_unit: FDA 510(k)/De Novo decisions for AI-enabled devices

evidence.title: PREDICTING POSTOPERATIVE OUTCOMES IN FULL-THICKNESS MACULAR HOLE REPAIR SURGERY: ChatGPT Versus Clinical Decision
evidence.outcome: Optimism bias and missed adverse outcomes in ChatGPT-5 predictions
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-5 failed to identify nonclosure; 0% accuracy for worsened cases, <=13% for stable; mean BCVA error 11.4 ± 10.8 letters, ~60% within two lines.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT achieved perfect accuracy in closure cases but failed to identify nonclosure, reflecting optimism bias.

evidence.title: FDA-Cleared Artificial Intelligence Medical Devices in Orthopaedic Surgery
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Global research & reviews
evidence.outcome: Share of FDA-cleared orthopaedic AI devices lacking clinical testing or validated prospectively
evidence.effect: 22.8% of 70 devices lacked clinical testing, 68.6% used retrospective data sets, and only 8.6% had a prospective clinical trial. Lack of clinical testing fell from 62.2% (2017-2019) to 19.7% (2022-2024).
evidence.quote: Overall, 22.8% of orthopaedic AIMDs lacked clinical testing and 68.6% were tested with retrospective data sets.

evidence.title: Human versus AI in audiological practice: A comparative evaluation of ChatGPT and physician treatment decisions in idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss
evidence.outcome: Clinical decision-making concordance with physicians for ISSNHL treatment
evidence.effect: ChatGPT's clinical decision-making for ISSNHL was inferior to experienced physicians, with frequent discordance and lack of individualized reasoning and context sensitivity.
evidence.quote: While ChatGPT (GPT-4o) shows promise in generating structured, protocol-driven suggestions, its clinical decision-making capabilities for ISSNHL remain inferior to those of experienced physicians.

commentary.bottom_line: Six studies test pre-pilot clinical validation, and most show that it can surface failures that benchmarks or image-quality scores missed, but none shows that validation reduces patient harm after deployment. The one outcome-linked study found a recall hazard ratio of 1.39 for devices without published clinical studies, with a credible interval that includes 1.

perspectives.view: Four of six tests are offline or simulated level 4 studies. The one outcome study is cross-sectional and imprecise (HR 1.39; 95% CrI, 0.84-3.52). Certainty is very low because of study design, indirectness, and imprecision. The studies suggest that validation detects model problems, but they do not show that detection changes patient outcomes.

Readers rated 32 of 33 AI-denoised PET images good or excellent, yet lesion sensitivity was 66%, and 62% of false positives were scored as definite lesions. A simulated nurse trial found severe potential risks from misleading AI despite favorable benchmarks. These results suggest that validation against clinical endpoints may catch failures that technical metrics hide.

In a real tumor board deployment, ChatGPT-4o concordance was 79.2%, below an 80% benchmark, and clinicians changed their view in 0 of 106 discussions. Knee MRI agreement ranged from 0.31 to 0.84 across 11 readers. Measured performance may depend on the reader and the workflow, so validation designs may need to include the intended users.

FDA draft guidance asks that validation characterize performance for the intended use. Public summaries stated clinical data for 70.6% of 1,491 AI device decisions. Among 70 orthopaedic devices, 22.8% lacked clinical testing, down from 62.2% in 2017-2019 to 19.7% in 2022-2024, and 8.6% had a prospective trial.

No study reports the cost or staff time of risk-scaled validation. The simulated nurse evaluation enrolled 462 participants and analyzed 4,125 case records. This suggests that human-in-the-loop testing for higher-risk tools may require substantial evaluator time. Scaling the evidence required to the level of risk, as the FDA generative AI paper describes, may allow lighter testing for lower-risk tools.

No test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, and two did not report a country. One hazard study of sudden hearing loss included patients with disability and found ChatGPT decisions often discordant with physician decisions. Validation results from these samples may not carry over to underserved groups.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares tools that underwent risk-scaled clinical validation before piloting with tools that did not, using patient harm, recalls, or pilot outcomes as endpoints. Future studies should test whether validation findings change deployment decisions. They should also test whether matching the scale of validation to the risk level affects downstream safety. These studies need samples that include underserved populations.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the six studies testing the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and two did not report a country. The evidence therefore cannot show whether validation detects failures that affect these groups. Health systems serving these patients may need to validate tools on their own populations.
